title: Start here
q: What does COMMIT promise?
opts: The log record is on disk
why: The data files catch up later, at a checkpoint. Replicas depend on the replication setting.

title: Start here
q: Why does an index lookup stay fast as a table grows?
opts: The index is kept in memory
A B+ tree is only a few levels deep
why: A lookup reads a few pages: root, branches and a leaf. Ten times more rows adds about one level at most.

title: Start here
q: In PostgreSQL at REPEATABLE READ and in InnoDB, when is the snapshot taken?
opts: At the first query in the transaction
why: Statements between BEGIN and the first query pin nothing. The MVCC lab on the Staff Path shows it.

title: Ten concepts
q: The primary is slow because of writes. Someone suggests adding two read replicas. In your own words, why will that not help, and what would?
ans:
Why not: every replica has to apply every write the primary makes. Replicas take reads off the primary; they do nothing for writes. They also add lag, so anything that reads its own writes from a replica may not see them.

What helps: making each write cheaper (fewer indexes, smaller rows, batching), moving writes that do not need to be there (sessions, counters) to a store built for them, and only then splitting the writes across several primaries.

title: PostgreSQL
q: You DELETE half the rows of a 10 GB table. What happens to the file size right away?
why: A DELETE marks row versions dead. VACUUM later makes the space reusable inside the file. The file only shrinks with a rewrite, such as VACUUM FULL.

title: PostgreSQL
q: With synchronous_commit = on, when does COMMIT return?
opts: After the table file is written
After the WAL is flushed to disk
why: The table file is written later, at a checkpoint. The WAL flush is what makes the commit durable.

title: PostgreSQL
q: What stops VACUUM from removing dead rows?
opts: An old transaction that is still open
why: An open snapshot may still need old versions. Notebook 1 showed 500,000 dead rows that VACUUM could not remove until it closed.

title: PostgreSQL
q: Where do a table's data files live?
why: pg_wal/ holds the WAL. base/ holds one directory per database, with a file per table and index.

title: PostgreSQL
q: A table takes 5,000 updates a second on the same 10,000 rows. The row count never changes, but the table file keeps growing. What is happening, and what do you check first?
ans:
What is happening: every UPDATE in PostgreSQL writes a new version of the row. The old version stays in the file as a dead row until vacuum removes it. If vacuum cannot keep up, or is not allowed to remove the dead rows, the file grows.

What I check first: whether something is holding back the cleanup. A transaction that has been open for hours, a session sitting idle in transaction, or a replication slot nobody reads all stop vacuum from removing rows that someone might still need. pg_stat_activity (oldest xact_start and backend_xmin) and pg_replication_slots show them. Then n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum in pg_stat_user_tables.

What I would change: end the long transaction first. Then make autovacuum visit this table more often with a lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on the table, and lower its fillfactor so updates that do not touch an indexed column can stay on the same page. Notebook 1 shows one open transaction taking a table from 5.8 MB to 29 MB.

title: PostgreSQL
q: How many pages does PostgreSQL read to find one row by its id, in a table of a million rows?
ans: Four: three index pages (root, branch, leaf) and the table page that holds the row. A million rows only needs a three-level index, which is why a lookup by key stays fast as the table grows.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: How are rows ordered inside an InnoDB table file?
why: The table is a clustered index on the primary key: the rows live in the leaves of that B+ tree.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: Which log does crash recovery replay?
why: Redo rebuilds the data pages. The binlog is for replicas and point-in-time recovery.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: One snapshot stays open while other sessions update rows. Which number grows?
why: Purge cannot remove undo records the old snapshot might need. In Notebook 1 it went from 11 to 20,006.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: Why do random UUID primary keys slow inserts down?
opts: New rows land on random pages across the clustered index
why: Each insert dirties a different page, and every secondary index stores the 16-byte key too. Time-ordered keys go to the end.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: You add an index on email to a large InnoDB table whose primary key is a UUID stored as CHAR(36). The new index is much bigger than the emails alone. Why, and what would you have done differently?
ans:
Why: in InnoDB, every secondary index entry stores the primary key as its pointer to the row. Each email entry carries the 36-character UUID with it. A lookup by email finds the primary key in the secondary index, then walks the clustered index to get the row.

The other cost: random UUIDs land all over the clustered index, so inserts split pages and the buffer pool holds more pages than it needs to.

What I would do: store the UUID as BINARY(16) with UUID_TO_BIN(uuid, 1), which also reorders a version 1 UUID by time. Or use a BIGINT auto-increment primary key and keep the UUID as a unique secondary column for the outside world. Every secondary index gets smaller either way. Watch the difference in Watch an index grow.

title: MySQL · InnoDB
q: How many pages does InnoDB read to find one row by its primary key, in a table of a million rows?
ans: Three: root, branch and leaf. In InnoDB the leaf holds the row itself, so there is no separate table page to read. PostgreSQL needs one more.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: With w: "majority" and the default journaling setting, when is a write acknowledged?
opts: When the primary has it in memory
When a majority of voting members have it in their journal
why: writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault is true by default, so majority writes wait for the journal on a majority.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: A secondary falls further behind than the oplog window. What happens?
opts: The primary pauses writes until it catches up
why: The oplog entries it needs have been overwritten, so it cannot catch up from the oplog.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: A multi-document transaction stays open past transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds. What happens?
opts: It waits until the client returns
why: In Notebook 1, the commit failed after the limit, and the write was gone.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: How does MongoDB store documents on disk?
opts: As compressed BSON inside WiredTiger files
why: Each collection and index is a .wt file, with BSON documents in compressed blocks.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: Reads were fine last month. Now p99 latency has tripled, with no code change and the same traffic. The data has grown past the WiredTiger cache. What changed, and what do you look at?
ans:
What changed: the pages your queries touch no longer all fit in the WiredTiger cache. Some reads now come from the operating system's file cache, which holds compressed pages, and some from disk. When the cache is full, application threads are also asked to help evict pages, which adds latency to ordinary queries.

What I look at: db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache: bytes in the cache against the maximum, pages read into the cache per second, and eviction by application threads. Then index sizes from db.collection.stats(), because indexes that no longer fit hurt every query.

What I would change: drop indexes nobody uses ($indexStats shows them), archive old documents, or add memory. Sharding is the answer only when the working set is too big for any one machine you would want to run.

title: MongoDB · WiredTiger
q: A write was acknowledged with w: 1, and the primary crashes a second later. Can the write be lost?
ans: Yes. With w: 1 the primary answered before any secondary had the write. If a secondary that never received it is elected, the write is rolled back. With w: "majority" it cannot be lost this way.

title: Redis
q: With appendfsync everysec, what can a power failure lose?
opts: About the last second of writes
why: Redis flushes the AOF about once a second in the background, so writes acknowledged in that second can be lost.

title: Redis
q: Why can one slow command slow down every client?
opts: Redis locks the whole keyspace on each write
One main thread runs commands one at a time
why: Commands run one after another on the main thread, which is also why each command is atomic.

title: Redis
q: Memory reaches maxmemory and the policy is noeviction, the default. What happens to a SET?
opts: An old key is evicted to make room
The write fails with an OOM error
why: noeviction refuses writes that need memory. For a cache, an LRU or LFU policy evicts instead.

title: Redis
q: Why can a snapshot on a busy 40 GB instance need much more than 40 GB?
opts: The snapshot is built in memory first
The forked child shares pages until the parent changes them, then each changed page is copied
why: Copy-on-write: the more the parent writes during the save, the more pages are duplicated.

title: Redis
q: Your sessions live in Redis with appendfsync everysec and one replica. The primary's machine loses power and the replica is promoted. What do users notice? Is that acceptable for sessions? For shopping carts?
ans:
What they notice: writes from about the last second can be gone, and more if the replica was lagging, because replication is asynchronous. Some people who just logged in are logged out; some last cart changes are missing.

Sessions: acceptable. The cost is a re-login.

Carts: annoying but survivable if the cart is rebuilt or the order is written to the relational database at checkout. Never keep the only copy of an order in Redis.

If it is not acceptable: use WAIT for the writes that matter, which narrows the window but does not close it, or keep that data in a database that waits for the disk and a standby.

title: Redis
q: A SET got OK from Redis with appendfsync everysec. Is it on disk yet?
ans: Not necessarily. Redis replies before the AOF is flushed, and the flush happens about once a second in the background. Tick the box in the widget to see what a power failure in that second does.

title: Cassandra
q: What decides which nodes store a row?
opts: A hash of the partition key
The node that received the write
why: The partition key is hashed to a token, and the token range decides the replicas.

title: Cassandra
q: Three replicas. You write at QUORUM and read at QUORUM. Does the read see the write?
opts: Yes: any two of three overlap with the two that took the write
why: Two plus two is more than three, so at least one node in the read has the write.

title: Cassandra
q: What is a tombstone?
opts: A marker that records a delete until compaction removes the data
A node that left the ring
why: Deletes are writes too. The marker stays for gc_grace_seconds so every replica learns about the delete.

title: Cassandra
q: Why must repair run within gc_grace_seconds?
opts: Otherwise a replica that missed a delete can bring the data back
why: Once the tombstone is gone, a replica that never saw the delete looks like the newest copy.

title: Cassandra
q: A chat app stores messages with PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, sent_at). One channel has 50 million messages, and reads for it are slow on the same few nodes. What is wrong, and what would you change?
ans:
What is wrong: the partition key is channel_id alone, so the whole channel is one partition on the same three replicas. At about 300 bytes a message that is roughly 15 GB in one partition: one hot set of nodes, long compactions, and reads that walk a huge partition.

What I would change: add a time bucket, PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, day), sent_at), or month for quieter channels, so each partition stays well under 100 MB. The app reads the latest bucket first and walks back.

And: old buckets can expire with a TTL and TimeWindow compaction, so retention is files being dropped, not millions of tombstones.

title: Cassandra
q: A replica is down and you write at QUORUM with three replicas. Does the write succeed?
ans: Yes. Two of three is a quorum. The coordinator keeps a hint for the missing replica. At consistency ALL the same write would fail. Tick the box in the widget to step through it.

title: Vector databases
q: What does hnsw.ef_search trade?
why: A bigger candidate list finds more of the true neighbours and takes a little longer.

title: Vector databases
q: Why did one tenant's search return 1.3 rows instead of 10 in Notebook 8?
opts: The filter ran after the index picked 40 candidates, most from other tenants
The tenant had only one row
why: The index does not know about the WHERE clause. Iterative scan, or an exact search inside the tenant, fixes it.

title: Vector databases
q: You switch to a new embedding model. What must happen to the stored vectors?
opts: Re-embed all of them with the new model
why: Vectors from different models live in different spaces; comparing them gives meaningless distances.

title: Vector databases
q: Going by Notebook 8, about how big is an HNSW index for 1 million 384-dimension vectors?
why: About 2,048 bytes per vector, so roughly 2 GB, and the table is as big again.

title: Vector databases
q: You have 20 million chunks with 1,536-dimension embeddings in pgvector, under an HNSW index. How much memory does the index want, and what would you do if the server has 128 GB?
ans:
The arithmetic: 20 million × 1,536 × 4 bytes is about 123 GB of vectors, and the index adds roughly 512 bytes of links each, about 10 GB more: around 133 GB for the index alone. It does not fit in 128 GB with anything else running.

What I would try, in order: store halfvec (2 bytes a dimension), which halves the index to around 72 GB. Check whether a model or setting with fewer dimensions loses anything on your own test questions. Partition by tenant so the hot part fits. Then consider a disk-based index or a dedicated vector store.

Every step: measure recall against an exact search on a sample before and after. Saving memory is only a win if the answers stay good.

title: Vector databases
q: An HNSW index over 100,000 vectors returns its 10 nearest in under a millisecond. At the default settings, what share of the true 10 nearest does it find?
ans: About 95% in Notebook 8, with ef_search at 40. Approximate means it usually finds them, not always. Raising ef_search to 160 found all of them for a little more time.

title: Engines side by side
q: After a crash, where does recovery start?
opts: From the last checkpoint, replaying the log after it
why: The data files are correct as of the checkpoint. The log after it holds everything committed since.

title: Engines side by side
q: In Notebook 6, 1,600 attempts tried to buy an item with 1,000 in stock by reading the stock and then writing the new value. How many sold?
why: All three engines oversold. A conditional update, WHERE available >= 1, sold exactly 1,000.

title: Engines side by side
q: Which MySQL setting trades a short window of acknowledged commits for speed?
why: With 1, every commit flushes the redo log. With 0 or 2, the flush happens about once a second.

title: Engines side by side
q: A new service does 2,000 small writes a second and must lose nothing on failover. In each engine, which settings make "lose nothing" true?
ans:
PostgreSQL: synchronous_commit = on (the default) plus a synchronous standby in synchronous_standby_names, and a failover tool that only promotes a synchronous standby, such as Patroni in synchronous mode.

MySQL: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1 and sync_binlog = 1, plus semi-synchronous replication with AFTER_SYNC, or Group Replication.

MongoDB: write concern w: "majority", the default since 5.0, with journaling.

The catch: in Notebook 2, one client doing fully durable commits managed about 4,200 a second on PostgreSQL, 1,770 on MySQL and about 1,100 on MongoDB. 2,000 a second needs several connections committing at once, so the engine can flush many commits together.

title: Engines side by side
q: Where does replication lag usually come from: the network, or the replica applying the change?
ans: Usually the replica applying it. Shipping a log record takes milliseconds; the replica replaying it can wait behind a long query, a huge transaction or a single busy apply thread. Tick the box in the widget to see each engine's version.

title: Database families
q: Which family suits heavy, steady, append-heavy writes?
why: Writes go to memory and sorted files, which disks handle well. Compaction merges them later.

title: Database families
q: Reports sum two columns over billions of rows. Which family?
why: It reads only the two columns, compressed. Notebook 7 read 870,400 of 10 million rows in 8 ms.

title: Database families
q: Why can one slow Redis command make every client wait?
opts: Commands run on one main thread
Redis writes to disk on every command
why: Each command is atomic for the same reason.

title: Queries that look fine and are not
q: The index is on (customer_id, created_at). A query filters on created_at alone. What happened in all three engines?
opts: A full scan of the table
why: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so rows for one date are spread across all of it.

title: Queries that look fine and are not
q: How many rows does OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20 read?
why: OFFSET reads and discards every skipped row. Paging by key read 20.

title: Queries that look fine and are not
q: How does PostgreSQL show that a query never touched the table?
opts: Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0
why: It needs the visibility map to be current, which VACUUM maintains.

title: Queries that look fine and are not
q: What makes N+1 queries slow when each query is fast?
why: 100 queries took 20.1 ms. One query with a list took 1.6 ms.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?
why: MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: MySQL at REPEATABLE READ, two read-then-write deposits on one row. What did the run show?
opts: An error on the second write
One deposit lost, with no error
why: An InnoDB UPDATE reads the latest committed row, not the snapshot, so the stale value overwrote the first deposit.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: Which run stopped write skew?
why: It failed the second commit with a serialization error. The application must retry.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: What is the simplest fix for a lost update on a counter?
opts: A relative update: SET n = n + 1
why: The engine applies it to the current value, so there is no stale read to lose.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: Which engines keep both deposits, at their default settings?
ans: None of them. PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED and MySQL at REPEATABLE READ silently kept 120. PostgreSQL at REPEATABLE READ and MongoDB in transactions refused the second write with an error, which keeps 110 and hands the retry to the application.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: Two sessions update the same account at the same moment, in PostgreSQL's default isolation level. What happens to the second one?
ans: It waits for the first to commit, then re-reads the row and applies its change on top. Both changes are kept. In REPEATABLE READ it would get an error instead and have to retry.

title: Lost updates and write skew
q: Which engine and level stops this?
ans: Only PostgreSQL at SERIALIZABLE. It tracks what each transaction read, notices the two depend on each other, and fails the second commit. Every other run ended with nobody on call.

title: Watch an index grow
q: you insert 300 rows with sequential ids, and 300 with random UUIDs. Which needs more pages, and roughly how many more?
ans: Random UUIDs need about a third more pages, and split far more often in the middle of the tree. Sequential ids only ever split the last page, so every page they leave behind is full. Random keys split pages in the middle, and both halves stay part-empty. Press "Compare all three key types" below to see it.

title: Lab notebooks
q: Notebook 2 shows durable commits costing about twice as much as non-durable ones, with one client. Why would that gap shrink with 50 clients committing at once?
ans:
Group commit: when many transactions commit at the same moment, the engine writes all their log records and flushes the log once for the whole group. One flush is shared by dozens of commits, so the cost of waiting for the disk is spread across them.

PostgreSQL, InnoDB with the binary log, and WiredTiger's journal all do this. That is why a single-client benchmark is the worst case for durability, and why the honest answer to "can we afford durable commits" is to measure it with your real concurrency.

title: Lab notebooks
q: PostgreSQL: 100,000 rows, a snapshot held open, then 500,000 row updates. How many dead row versions can VACUUM remove while the snapshot is open?
ans: None of the 500,000. VACUUM says so itself: "500000 are dead but not yet removable". Once the snapshot is released, the same VACUUM removes all of them, and the file stays at 29 MB.

title: Lab notebooks
q: How much faster are commits when they do not wait for the log flush: 10 percent, 2 times, or 10 times?
ans: On this machine, about 1.8 times in PostgreSQL, 2.3 times in MySQL and 2.6 times in MongoDB. On a disk where a flush costs more, such as network-attached storage, the gap is larger. Measure on your own disk before you decide.

title: Lab notebooks
q: With an index on email, how many 8 KB pages does PostgreSQL read to find one row out of a million?
ans: Four: shared hit=1 read=3. Without the index it read 19,231, every page of the 150 MB table.

title: Lab notebooks
q: Two sessions each read a balance of 100 and add to it, +10 and +20. With the default settings, does PostgreSQL keep both deposits?
ans: No. At READ COMMITTED, the default, the final balance is 120, and the +10 is lost. At REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL refuses the second update instead.

title: Lab notebooks
q: The index is on (customer_id, created_at). A query filters only on created_at. Does any of the three engines use the index?
ans: None of them did. PostgreSQL and MySQL scanned the whole table, and MongoDB did a COLLSCAN, because the index is sorted by customer_id first.

title: Lab notebooks
q: Sixteen clients try 1,600 purchases of an item with 1,000 in stock. Each one reads the stock, and if it is above zero, writes the stock minus one. How many sales go through?
ans: All 1,600, in every engine, and the stock still shows hundreds left. The conditional update, UPDATE ... WHERE available >= 1, sold exactly 1,000 and left 0.

title: Lab notebooks
q: ClickHouse holds 10,000,000 order lines. A revenue report filters on one month and sums two columns. How many rows does it read?
ans: 870,400 rows and about 15 MB, in 8 ms. The table is partitioned by month and sorted by SKU and time, so ClickHouse skipped every part that could not match and read only the columns the query names.

title: Lab notebooks
q: One tenant's memories are 1% of the table. You ask for that tenant's 10 nearest memories with WHERE tenant_id = ? and LIMIT 10, using the HNSW index with the default ef_search of 40. How many rows come back?
ans: 1.3 on average, not 10. The index found its 40 nearest candidates across all tenants, then the filter threw away the 99% that belonged to someone else. Turning on iterative scan returned all 10.

title: Anti-patterns
q: A teammate wants to store each product's tag ids as a JSON array in the product row, to avoid a join table. When is that fine, and when does it hurt?
ans:
Fine when: the tags are always read and written together with the product, nobody asks "which products have tag 42", and only one process edits them.

It hurts when: you need that reverse query. It needs a GIN index in PostgreSQL or a multi-valued index in MySQL 8.0, and it is still harder to get right than a join table. Nothing stops a deleted tag id from staying in the array. And two people adding a tag at the same time read the array, change it and write it back, so one change is lost.

What I would do: a join table, product_tags (product_id, tag_id) with a primary key on both. It is boring, and it answers every question.

title: What a commit waits for
q: Your only synchronous standby goes down at 2 a.m. What happens to writes on the primary, and what could you have set up instead?
ans:
PostgreSQL: if synchronous_standby_names names only that standby, every commit waits for it and the application hangs. The commits are durable on the primary, but no client gets an acknowledgement.

MySQL: semi-synchronous replication waits rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout (10 seconds by default) and then quietly falls back to asynchronous. Writes carry on, without the guarantee.

What I would set up: two standbys with ANY 1 (a, b), so either one can acknowledge. Or Patroni's synchronous mode, which drops to asynchronous on purpose and refuses to fail over to a standby that might be behind. Decide in daylight which you want: stop writing, or keep writing without the guarantee.

title: Where to run the database
q: Which job stays yours in every option, including managed?
why: The provider can take backups. Only you can prove a restore works for your data. The schema stays yours too.

title: Where to run the database
q: Can the standby of an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance serve reads?
why: It is a synchronous standby for failover. For reads, use a read replica or a Multi-AZ DB cluster.

title: Where to run the database
q: An Aurora Serverless v2 database paused at zero capacity. What does the first connection see?
opts: A resume that typically takes about 15 seconds
An error until someone resumes it
why: Longer after a day of sleep. Set client timeouts and retries for it.

title: On-prem vs cloud, by engine
q: Your team has two engineers who know databases, and a growing PostgreSQL on EC2. Do you move to a managed service or keep running it yourselves? What decides it?
ans:
Count the jobs, not the hourly price: backups and tested restores, failover, minor and major upgrades, OS patching, monitoring, and someone on call every night. Two people cannot share a night rotation for long.

Managed wins when those jobs are what is eating the team's time. It costs more per hour and buys back the jobs.

Self-managed wins when you need something the service does not allow (an extension, superuser, a specific version), or the load is large and steady enough that the price difference pays for more people. Either way, write down who does each job before you decide.

title: Capacity calculator
q: Your estimate says 3,000 writes a second at peak. Before you trust it, which two numbers do you measure on real hardware, and how?
ans:
1. The cost of one durable commit on your storage, with your real durability settings. pgbench or sysbench with one client and then with many, like Notebook 2. Network storage can be several times slower than the numbers you have in your head.

2. The real size of a row and its indexes. Load a million rows that look like production, then divide the table plus index size by the row count. The estimate's bytes-per-row is the number most often wrong by two or three times.

Then check the peak-to-average ratio against real traffic logs, not a guess.

title: Why the bill is huge
q: The database bill doubled in a month and the traffic did not. Name the first three things you would check, in order.
ans:
1. Storage and backups: table and index growth (bloat counts), snapshot retention, and logs kept longer than anyone meant. In PostgreSQL, pg_total_relation_size on the largest tables; in the bill, storage and backup lines.

2. I/O: a new report, export or missing index that scans a big table every few minutes. On I/O-billed storage, such as Aurora Standard, that shows up directly as cost.

3. Data transfer: a new replica in another zone or region, or an application now reading across zones. Replication traffic is billed every day, quietly.

Then instance size changes. Cost Explorer grouped by usage type usually points at one of these in a few minutes.

title: Migration playbooks
q: You are moving a 2 TB MySQL database to a new cluster with under a minute of write downtime. Outline the steps.
ans:
Copy: a physical copy, such as XtraBackup or a cloned replica, restored on the new cluster. Note its GTID position.

Catch up: make the new cluster a replica of the old one from that position. Let it catch up, then compare the data with checksums (pt-table-checksum or similar). Send some read traffic to it and compare answers.

Cut over: set the old primary read_only, wait until the new one has applied every GTID, then switch the application through the proxy or DNS you lowered the TTL on beforehand. Writes are paused only for those seconds.

Keep a way back: replicate from the new cluster to the old one for a while, so rolling back is another switch, not a restore.

title: Store orders and inventory
q: A flash sale puts 20,000 shoppers on one product in the first minute. Every checkout updates the same stock row. What breaks first, and what would you change?
ans:
The arithmetic: 20,000 in 60 seconds is about 333 updates a second on one row. Each one holds that row's lock for 5 ms until it commits, so the row can take at most 200 a second.

What happens: the queue grows by about 133 checkouts every second. Connections pile up waiting on the lock, the pool runs dry, and pages that never touch this product slow down too.

What I would change: keep the lock as short as possible: one UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, committed straight away, with payment outside the transaction. For bigger sales, split the stock into several rows and take from any one with stock left.

Try other numbers →

title: Payments and ledgers
q: Finance wants every merchant's balance at month end. There are 50,000 merchants. Do you add up the ledger, or keep a balance, and how do you prove the two agree?
ans:
The arithmetic: one month of ledger is about 60 million rows. Adding them up per merchant works, but a balance read on every payment would mean summing all of history, which is 5,110 million rows by the end of the retention period.

What I would do: keep a balance row per account and change it in the same transaction as the ledger entries, so they can never disagree after a commit. The ledger stays the source of truth.

Proving it: a nightly job sums the day's entries per account and compares the total with the change in the balance row. Any difference pages someone. Entries are never updated or deleted; a mistake is fixed with a new reversing entry.

Try other numbers →

title: Bookings and reservations
q: A concert goes on sale: 100,000 fans, 5,000 seats, and most of the seats go in the first two minutes. Where is the pressure, and how do you hand out seats without double booking?
ans:
The arithmetic: 5,000 seats in 120 seconds is about 42 bookings a second, which any primary handles. 100,000 fans refreshing the seat map every few seconds is about 33,333 reads a second, which is the real load.

What I would change: serve the seat map from a cache refreshed every second or two, so it is allowed to be slightly wrong. Put people in a waiting room in front of the booking step.

Handing out seats: each hold is one short transaction: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a free seat, mark it held with an expiry 10 minutes out, commit. Two fans never get the same row, and nobody waits on a lock someone else holds. A unique constraint on (event, seat) for paid bookings is the last line of defence.

title: Accounts and sessions
q: The session store restarts and loses every session. What happens in the next minute, and what would you put in place before it happens?
ans:
The arithmetic: about 2,000,000 live sessions disappear. If only one in ten of those users comes back in the next minute, that is 3,333 logins a second. A password hash is built to be slow, roughly 100 ms of CPU each, so that needs about 333 CPU cores just for hashing.

What happens: the login service saturates, login requests time out, users retry, and the account database takes the extra reads as well.

What I would change: run the session store with a replica and persistence so a restart is not a wipe. Use long-lived refresh tokens so most users get a new session without a password. Rate limit logins per user and keep spare capacity for this day.

title: Multi-tenant SaaS
q: Your largest customer is 300 times the size of the average one and asks for their own database. Shared tables, a schema per tenant, or a database per tenant?
ans:
The arithmetic: a schema per tenant means 80,000 tables, and every migration runs once per tenant: at 2 seconds a tenant that is 66.7 min per change, with some tenants on the new schema and some on the old one in between.

What I would do: keep most tenants in shared tables with tenant_id first in every primary key and index, and row-level security as a backstop. Move the largest tenant to its own cluster running the same schema. That is a database per tenant for the few who need it, without paying for it 2,000 times.

What to plan for: a tenant directory that says which cluster each tenant lives on, so moving one later is a data copy and a directory update.

title: Product catalog
q: Marketing reprices 2 million products in one job. What does that do to the replicas, the cache and the search index?
ans:
The arithmetic: 2 million updates of a 4 KB document write about 9.6 GB of WAL or oplog, because the whole row or document is logged. At 2,000 updates a second the job takes about 16.7 min.

What happens: if the job runs as fast as it can, replicas fall behind and customers on a replica see old prices. Two million cache entries go stale at once, and the search index has a backlog of 2 million documents to reindex.

What I would change: run it in batches of a few thousand with a pause, watching replica lag. Keep prices in their own small table or document so a price change does not rewrite the whole product. Invalidate the cache from the change stream rather than from the job.

title: Social feed
q: An account with 20 million followers posts ten times in one hour, at peak. What happens to the fan-out work, and what would you change?
ans:
The arithmetic: 10 posts × 20,000,000 followers = 200 million timeline writes in an hour, about 55,556 a second, on top of the normal peak of 3,472 a second.

What happens: the fan-out queue backs up for that whole hour, and every follower of every other account waits behind it.

What I would change: no fan-out above a follower threshold. Those posts are merged into the timeline when a reader opens it. Most feeds end up as a hybrid of the two.

title: Search and AI retrieval
q: Product wants to move from 768 to 3,072 dimensions for better answers. What happens to memory, and does it change where the vectors live?
ans:
The arithmetic: the index goes from about 57.3 GB to about 205 GB, 3.6 times as much, for the same 16,000,000 vectors.

What happens: it still fits on one server, but rebuilding the index takes longer and every insert costs more.

What I would check first: measure whether the answers actually get better on your own questions. If they do, try quantized vectors or a model that lets you cut dimensions before moving to a separate vector store. Keep the documents and permissions in the relational database either way.

title: Chat and messaging
q: One announcement goes out to a 100,000-member channel. How many writes is that, and how would you avoid most of them?
ans:
The arithmetic: copying the message into every member's inbox is 100,000 writes and about 15 MB of rows for one message. Doing it a few times an hour is fine; doing it for every busy channel is not.

What I would change: store the message once, in the channel's history. Each member keeps one row with the last message they have read. Unread counts come from comparing that pointer with the channel's latest message id.

Delivery: push the message to members who are online over their open connection. Members who are offline see it when they next open the channel. Only small direct conversations get a copy per person, if at all.

title: IoT and telemetry
q: Someone asks to keep raw readings for two years instead of 30 days. What does that cost, and what would you offer instead?
ans:
The arithmetic: one day of raw readings is about 5.2 GB on disk, so two years is about 3.8 TB, 24.3 times today's storage.

What I would offer: raw readings for 30 days, then one-minute rollups (min, max, average, count) kept for two years. That is one row per device per minute instead of 6, about 37.8 TB for two years, 0.1 times smaller.

How: partition by day so expiring raw data is dropping a partition, not deleting rows. Build the rollups as data arrives, with a materialized view or a scheduled job.

title: Audit and event logs
q: Legal asks for every event touching one customer over 7 years. How long does that take, and what makes it fast?
ans:
The arithmetic: without an index on the customer, the query reads all 51.1 TB. At about 1 GB a second that is 14.2 hours, and it competes with the writes the whole time.

What makes it fast: an index on (customer_id, created_at) in each monthly partition. The query becomes 84 small index lookups, one per partition, which is seconds rather than 14.2 hours.

What else: older partitions can move to cheaper storage or a column store, keeping the same index. Make the table insert-only through permissions, so nobody can quietly change history.

title: Leaderboards and counters
q: A streamer sends a million viewers to press "like" on one counter within ten seconds. One key, one Redis shard. What happens, and what would you change?
ans:
The arithmetic: 1,000,000 presses in 10 seconds is 100,000 increments a second on one key. One key lives on one shard and one core, so that shard is full, and every other key on it slows down.

What I would change: count in the application first. Each app server adds up the likes it receives and sends one INCRBY a second. With 50 servers that is 50 writes a second instead of 100,000. The count on screen is up to a second behind, which nobody notices.

If one place is not enough: split the counter into several keys on different shards, such as likes:{id}:0 to likes:{id}:15, and add them up when reading.

title: Analytics and reporting
q: Someone points the revenue dashboard at the primary PostgreSQL instead of the column store, "just for now". What does one 30-day query cost there?
ans:
The arithmetic: a row store reads whole rows, so a 30-day query reads about 600 GB. The column store reads about 11.3 GB for the same answer, 53 times less. At about 1 GB a second, the primary spends 10 min on each refresh.

What happens: the query pushes the hot pages of the application out of the cache, so checkout and login get slower while the dashboard loads. Ten people opening the dashboard at 9 a.m. is ten of these at once.

What I would change: keep reporting on the column store and feed it from the primary with change data capture. If a quick report has to come from PostgreSQL, run it on a replica with a statement timeout.

title: Agent memory and state
q: An enterprise customer asks you to delete everything the agent knows about one of their users, within 30 days. Where does that data live in this design, and how do you show it is gone?
ans:
Where it lives: about 300 memory rows with their embeddings, around 5,400 tool-call rows if that user ran agents every day for three months, the checkpoints of those runs, anything still in Redis, the run log exported to object storage, and every backup taken since. An embedding made from the user's words counts as their data too.

What makes it possible: tenant_id and the user's id on every table, so each delete is one indexed statement, not a search through JSON. Exported months stored per tenant, so you can rewrite one file instead of all of them. Backups that expire within the 30 days, so you can say when the last copy disappears.

How you show it: run the deletes as one recorded job, keep a log that says what was deleted and when (without the data itself), and answer the customer with that log and the date the last backup expires.
